steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Light direction dramatically changes a subject: front light = flat, even; side light = texture and depth; back light = rim lighting or silhouette.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Light quality: hard light (direct sun, bare flash) creates sharp shadows; soft light (overcast, softbox) creates gentle gradients.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The golden hour (just after sunrise/before sunset) produces warm, directional, soft light — ideal for many subjects.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Flash can fill shadows, freeze motion or be the primary light source — but on-camera flash creates flat, unflattering light.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Create a series of experimental studies exploring lighting and flash. Annotate your process. | Research an artist or designer who works with lighting and flash. Write a critical analysis of their approach and explain how it has informed your own work. | Evaluate the effectiveness of your experiments with lighting and flash. Which approaches were most successful and why?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A range of experimental studies showing different approaches to lighting and flash, each annotated with media, technique and purpose. Show development from initial experiments to refined outcomes. | A critical analysis naming a specific artist/designer, using specialist vocabulary, explaining their context and approach, and making clear connections to personal work. | A reflective evaluation identifying successful and less successful experiments, explaining WHY using technical and conceptual language, and showing how evaluation led to further refinement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Address ALL four Assessment Objectives — AO1 (develop), AO2 (refine), AO3 (record), AO4 (present) Show the FULL creative journey — from initial research to final outcome Annotate your work using specialist vocabulary (not just "I like it") Draw from primary sources wherever possible — real objects, not photos Experiment with a RANGE of media and techniques before selecting Make clear connections between artist research and your own developing work
